planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in any well-drained soil, siting in full sun for the heaviest fruit set.

directions: Sunrise Ruby is a Korean-origin goumi selection valued for fruit noticeably larger than the wild type, with the classic silver-speckled red skin and a sweet-tart flavor that mellows as the berries fully color in early summer. Like other goumi, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules and tolerates lean, sandy soils poorly suited to most fruiting shrubs, so avoid heavy fertilizing which can suppress fruiting. Plant alongside another goumi cultivar such as Sweet Scarlet or Tillamook to improve cross-pollination and yield. Harvest by hand once berries detach easily and have lost most of their astringency.
sources: Burnt Ridge Nursery — Sunrise Ruby Goumi
University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension — Goumi Berry Production

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in any well-drained soil; confirm local legality before planting, as autumn olive is regulated as invasive in parts of the eastern U.S.

directions: Ruby is a named fruit-production selection of autumn olive bearing some of the largest fruit of the improved cultivars, with abundant bright red, silver-speckled berries carrying a tart-to-sweet flavor that sweetens further after a light frost. Like seedling autumn olive it is an aggressive nitrogen-fixing shrub that thrives in poor, sandy, or disturbed soils where few other fruiting plants succeed, but it spreads readily by seed via bird dispersal, so site it where volunteer seedlings can be managed. Harvest by stripping ripe clusters by hand in fall for fresh eating, juice, or fruit leather. Because it remains Elaeagnus umbellata, it carries the same invasive-species restrictions as the wild species in many eastern states.
sources: Burnt Ridge Nursery — Ruby Autumn Olive

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in any well-drained soil; this selection is self-fertile but crops more heavily with a second autumn olive nearby.

directions: Sweet 'n' Tart is a fruit-quality autumn olive selection chosen for unusually large berries and a balanced sugar-acid flavor, described by growers as tart on first bite and sweetening within moments — a notable improvement over the puckering astringency of unselected wild seedlings. The shrub flowers heavily on fragrant, cream-colored blossoms in late spring before setting silver-speckled red fruit in early autumn, and like all Elaeagnus it fixes nitrogen through root nodules, allowing it to thrive in poor or sandy soil. Harvest ripe berries by hand for fresh eating, jam, or fruit leather, and confirm local regulations before planting since autumn olive is classified as invasive in parts of the eastern United States.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in any well-drained soil; confirm local legality before planting, as autumn olive is regulated as invasive in parts of the eastern U.S.

directions: Cardinal is an older, widely planted autumn olive selection originally distributed for conservation plantings, producing abundant small, red, silver-speckled berries that cluster tightly along the stem. It is among the hardiest and most vigorous of the fruiting selections, tolerating poor, dry, and sandy sites via its nitrogen-fixing root nodules, and it grows into a notably large, dense shrub at maturity. Birds spread the seed readily, so plant where seedling spread can be managed or contained. Harvest ripe fruit by hand-stripping clusters in fall; flavor improves and astringency drops after a light frost.
sources: USDA Soil Conservation Service plant release records

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in any well-drained soil; confirm local legality before planting, as autumn olive is regulated as invasive in parts of the eastern U.S.

directions: Jewel is a fruit-quality autumn olive selection noted by growers for berries that are smaller than some other named cultivars but unusually high in flavor and deep red color, with notably high lycopene content among autumn olive selections. It shares the species' tolerance for poor, sandy, or disturbed soils through its nitrogen-fixing root nodules, and sets a heavy crop of tart-sweet fruit in early fall that improves after a light frost. Birds disperse the seed readily, so site it where volunteer seedlings can be monitored and removed. Harvest by hand-stripping ripe clusters for fresh eating, juice, or fruit leather.
